Title: One-person ownership leaves critical work without backup
Mitigation: List primary and backup owners for the data pipeline, API, interface and deployment. Have the backup follow the clean-checkout steps and record what still depends on the primary owner.
Linked work: Relates: SCRUM-531; Relates: SCRUM-532; Relates: SCRUM-517
Description: Only one person knows pulls/model/UI; bus factor = 1.
Comments:
Actions:
* Shared the Jupyter notebooks, ML scripts and backend/UI code between both team members using the Git repo.
* Documented how to run the backend and front-end (requirements, commands, sample data) so either person can demo.
Result:
* Dependency on a single person is reduced; either team member can start the app and walk through the key flows.
Assessment:
* Probability reduced (but risk still present).
* Impact remains significant if it happens, so we keep this risk under monitoring.

The shared repository contains setup instructions, but this card has no current evidence that a second person can run the full stack. Keep a named backup and record a successful handoff before treating the dependency as reduced.

Title: Extra features delay required release work
Mitigation: Prioritize the failing core workflows and required submission corrections. Put optional features in the backlog and agree which existing task moves out when a new task moves in.
Description: Fancy visuals or features added without time budget.
Comments:
Actions:
* Explicitly de-scoped several “nice to have” items (advanced coach UI, SHAP explanations, extra visualizations).
* Focused this iteration on making the baseline ranking, Data Explorer, and Top-K tactics board stable and demoable.
Result:
* Core features for the defence are implemented; extra items are moved into future PBIs and later sprints.
Assessment:
* Probability reduced, but scope creep remains a  risk.
* We will keep parking new ideas into the backlog

The backlog already includes data repair, exports and cloud Gameplan work. Adding more features before the failed workflows are addressed would put the remaining release work at risk.

Title: Late requirement changes force rework
Mitigation: Record each new requirement against its affected story, model or test. Estimate its effect on the remaining schedule and confirm scope changes in the shared plan.
Linked work: Relates: SCRUM-528; Relates: SCRUM-529; Relates: SCRUM-530; Relates: SCRUM-465
Description: Supervisor requests live data or extra models close to deadline.
Comments:
Actions:
* Reviewed professor feedback and rubric again before planning this iteration.
* Aligned Jira backlog and sprints with the Elaboration Release requirements (ML comparison, Jira boards, Validation model).
Result:
* No major requirement changes arrived late in the iteration; any new suggestions were treated as future backlog items.
Assessment:
* Probability now low for this release.
* Impact would be high if it happened, but current iteration was stable.

The supervisor has requested further model, risk and test-plan corrections. These changes need explicit tasks and acceptance criteria so they do not silently displace the planned feature work.

Title: Coaches may not use or trust the recommendations
Mitigation: Observe scouting, matchup and late-game scenarios with a coach or identified proxy. Record confusing steps and whether the result supports a concrete decision.
Description: Tool isn’t used due to complexity or lack of trust.
Comments:
Actions:
* Simplified the UI so that Data Explorer shows raw, understandable stats instead of confusing ML columns.
* Designed the Top-K cards and one-page tactics board specifically for quick coach use (clear labels, PPP_baseline).
Result:
* The product is easier to explain and demo to non-technical users (coaches, analysts).
Assessment:
* Probability reduced to low–medium.
* Impact is moderate; we will watch feedback from demo sessions.

The app has coaching workflows, but there is no current coach acceptance result on this card. Working controls and readable labels alone do not establish that coaches would use the recommendations.

Title: Protected APIs may allow unauthorized access
Mitigation: Maintain a route and role matrix. Repeat missing-session, invalid-token and wrong-role checks after access changes, and restrict any route that accepts an unauthorized request.
Description:
Risk: Application or API operations intended for authenticated or authorized users may remain accessible without the required session or role.
Trigger: An unauthenticated, expired-session, or wrong-role request succeeds where the approved access policy requires rejection.
Assessment: Low probability is retained provisionally; propose Serious impact because the current model includes authenticated coach/analyst access. Endpoint reduction alone does not establish authorization.
Comments:
Actions:
* Reviewed the baseline API endpoints and limited them to only what is required for the UI.
* Ensured we are not exposing raw admin or internal operations endpoints in the demo app.
Result:
* Surface area of the API is smaller; endpoints are more focused on read-only data for the demo.
Assessment:
* Probability now low for this academic deployment.
* Impact would be high in production, but acceptable for the controlled capstone environment.

Elaboration review: probability Low; impact Serious. Reviewed the assessment and updated the mitigation plan.
Next action: Run the model’s relevant session, role, and permission checks against the current deployment, including invalid tokens and development-bypass configuration.
Current mitigation result: not established by this planning update; record the actual observation after the check.
Next review: within seven days, or sooner if the trigger occurs.

The recorded session and role checks rejected unauthorized requests. That supports the current access controls, but new routes still need the same checks; a resolved label would hide that ongoing exposure.

Title: Private tokens may be exposed in source or logs
Mitigation: Scan tracked changes and client output before sharing a release. Store server keys only in private configuration and rotate any key whose exposure is confirmed.
Description: Auth token or keys committed to Git or exposed in logs.
Comments:
Actions:
* Confirmed that any secrets (API keys, tokens) are kept in local configuration and NOT committed to the Git repo.
* Checked the repository history for accidental commits of secrets.
Result:
* No known secret leaks in the project repository.
Assessment:
* Probability currently low.
* Impact remains high if a leak ever happens, so we keep verifying before sharing code or doing public demos.

Private runtime settings are kept outside the tracked source, but the earlier comment does not prove the current client build and repository history are free of secrets. Keep the risk under monitoring until the release checks are recorded.

Title: Exported values may differ from API results
Mitigation: Use the same calculation and filters for each output format. Compare JSON, CSV and PDF values on a fixed dataset and record the dataset version with the export test.
Linked work: Relates: SCRUM-484; Relates: SCRUM-485; Relates: SCRUM-519; Relates: SCRUM-486; Relates: SCRUM-616
Description: JSON responses differ from CSV/Parquet due to version drift or rounding.
Comments:
Actions:
* Compared sample outputs from the /rank-plays/baseline endpoint with the original baseline notebook outputs.
* Ran spot checks on PPP_baseline values for a few teams and seasons.
Result:
* Numbers between the API and underlying files are consistent on sampled checks.
Assessment:
* Probability reduced to medium.
* Impact remains high; we will re-check if we update the dataset or baseline logic.

The recorded uplift checks compare JSON and CSV values successfully. The later unified export endpoint is still planned, so its rounding, filters and totals need separate checks when implemented.

The new exports must match the results already shown on Matchup, Context and Model Metrics. BST-171 through BST-178 now cover the three formats, selected context, stale results and file contents. These checks are still waiting for the deployed export change.

The Matchup, Context and Model Metrics exports matched the displayed rows. Testing found a negative-margin filename issue; SCRUM-616 fixed it and BST-178 passed the retest. The export checks now cover CSV, JSON and PDF.

Title: Missing models may break the baseline fallback
Mitigation: Test a controlled missing-model case outside production. Confirm the supported baseline fallback and show a clear error for workflows that cannot safely fall back.
Description: If ML fails, baseline isn’t used automatically, causing outages.
Comments:
Actions:
* Implemented and manually tested the behaviour where the UI and ranking logic can use baseline PPP if ML predictions are unavailable.
* Ensured Data Explorer and Top-K cards can still run purely on baseline data.
Result:
* System remains usable even without the ML model, so baseline fallback works for demo purposes.
Assessment:
* Probability now low that the app becomes unusable due to missing ML.
* Impact reduced to medium because the baseline-only experience is acceptable for the defence.

Baseline recommendations passed the recorded live checks. A successful normal request does not show how every model-dependent page behaves when an artifact is missing.

Title: Core pages may fail on supported browsers or screen sizes
Mitigation: Choose supported browser and viewport combinations, then repeat login, explorer, ranking and export flows. Fix clipped controls and unreadable results before expanding the supported set.
Description:
Risk: New interface changes may cause clipping, inaccessible controls, or broken workflows on supported browsers and screen sizes.
Trigger: A supported browser or viewport cannot complete a core task or displays unreadable/overlapping content.
Assessment: historical UI testing does not cover later changes.
Comments:
Actions:
* Simplified the layout for the main pages (Home, Data Explorer, Baseline/Top-K, Glossary).
* Tested the UI in at least two browsers and on different resolutions (laptop + external monitor).
Result:
* No major layout breaks found for the target demo environment.
Assessment:
* Probability now low.
* Impact is moderate; minor cosmetic issues are acceptable as long as flows work.

Elaboration review: probability Moderate; impact Tolerable. Reviewed the assessment and updated the mitigation plan.
Next action: Retest the current login, explorer, ranking, and export views at the agreed screen sizes.
Current mitigation result: not established by this planning update; record the actual observation after the check.
Next review: within seven days, or sooner if the trigger occurs.

The recent audit exercised browser workflows but did not certify all supported browsers or screen sizes. Keep layout compatibility open until the release has a defined browser and viewport checklist.

Title: Gameplan inputs may be ignored or incorrectly validated
Mitigation: Use one validated parsed context for every downstream request. Add first-click, boundary, overtime and unsupported-input cases and keep the failing case linked to its repair.
Linked work: Relates: SCRUM-539; Relates: SCRUM-540; Relates: SCRUM-541
Description:
Risk: Unsupported seasons, team selections, context values, or limits may pass validation and cause errors or misleading rankings.
Trigger: An invalid or unsupported input is accepted silently, causes an unhandled exception, or returns misleading output.
Assessment: one invalid request should not produce unsupported analytics.
Comments:
Actions:
* Added validation on the backend for required fields (season, team, opponent, k) on the baseline endpoints.
* Tightened the UI to only allow valid season ranges and known teams/opponents.
Result:
* Fewer chances of crashing the app or sending invalid queries from the front-end.
Assessment:
* Probability reduced from high to medium.
* Impact is medium; we will revisit if we add more complex filters.

Elaboration review: probability Low; impact Serious. Reviewed the assessment and updated the mitigation plan.
Next action: Execute the existing invalid-team, same-team, invalid-K, missing-input, and context-boundary cases appropriate to the current requirements.
Current mitigation result: not established by this planning update; record the actual observation after the check.
Next review: within seven days, or sooner if the trigger occurs.

The Gameplan audit found that the first Build can use the previous numeric context and that overtime is clamped to quarter 4. Those are concrete input-handling failures, so this risk should be active.

Title: Recommendation explanations may be unclear
Mitigation: State when a recommendation uses baseline data without game context. Keep each explanation tied to displayed values, repeat BST-97–99 after the change and ask a reviewer to explain the recommendation and its limits.
Linked work: Relates: SCRUM-536; Relates: SCRUM-497; Relates: SCRUM-498; Relates: SCRUM-546
Description: Rationale text is too technical or long; causes confusion.
Comments:
Actions:
* Updated the UI wording and Glossary to focus on simple concepts (PPP_baseline, play-type ranking) instead of ML jargon.
* Deferred advanced explanation/SHAP features to future PBIs to avoid overwhelming users now.
Result:
* Current explanations for baseline and Top-K recommendations are more coach-friendly.
Assessment:
* Probability reduced to medium.
* Impact is medium; explanation quality still depends on how we present it in the live demo.

The current rationale uses deterministic templates, and the glossary explains the metrics. There is still no recorded coach review showing that the wording makes the recommendation clear.

The five baseline explanations returned for TOR against BOS did not say that score, period and clock were not applied. Their numbers matched the ranking output, but the missing-context notice required by BST-99 is absent. Add that notice and repeat the explanation checks; coach comprehension still needs the planned stakeholder review.

Title: Deployed analysis requests exceed usable response times
Mitigation: Serve saved evaluation results for ordinary page visits. Profile slow requests, set bounded loading and error states, and rerun the recorded timeout case after the fix.
Description: Baseline >2s or ML >5s harms usability during short breaks.
Comments:
Actions:
* Measured response times for the baseline ranking endpoint with typical season/team/opponent filters.
* Kept data size reasonable by focusing on a limited number of seasons for the demo.
Result:
* Response times are acceptable for the interactive demo (well under several seconds on local dev).
Assessment:
* Probability now low for the current dataset size.
* Impact is medium if we scale up; for this release, latency is not a blocker.

The default Shot Model Metrics request reached the server's 300-second limit and returned 504. The earlier local latency result does not cover this deployed workflow.

Title: Metric labels may imply unsupported accuracy
Mitigation: Use consistent units and definitions in the API, page and report. Show the prediction target, baseline and evaluation period alongside each result.
Linked work: Relates: SCRUM-476; Relates: SCRUM-498; Relates: SCRUM-526
Description:
Risk: PPP, MAE, RMSE, uplift, accuracy, or probability may be conflated, causing incorrect interpretation of results.
Trigger: The report, API, or UI gives different meanings or units for the same metric, or labels a regression metric as classification accuracy.
Assessment: definitions must match the actual prediction target and evaluation task.
Comments:
Actions:
* Clarified in the report and notes that RMSE/uplift are used for technical evaluation, while PPP_baseline is the main metric shown to coaches.
* Ensured the UI does not mix MAE/uplift with coach-facing screens.
Result:
* Better separation between “coach metrics” and “data science metrics”.
Assessment:
* Probability now low.
* Impact low–medium; confusion risk is minimized for the demo audience.

Elaboration review: probability Low; impact Tolerable. Reviewed the assessment and updated the mitigation plan.
Next action: Check one evaluation table and its corresponding UI/API output against the metric dictionary.
Current mitigation result: not established by this planning update; record the actual observation after the check.
Next review: within seven days, or sooner if the trigger occurs.

The calibration page reports PPP bias, MAE and RMSE with its retrospective-data limitation. The report and glossary must preserve that meaning rather than describing these numbers as future-game accuracy.

The new [forecast report](https://github.com/Basketball-Capstone-25/NBAPlayRanker/blob/ba814406a69c6de23f14af06a28f153eaa436fdc/docs/iteration-15/forecast/README.md) labels MAE, RMSE and bias in PPP and states that it predicts a season ahead. It does not present these as classification accuracy or predictions before individual games. Keep Monitoring as these results are reused in the app or presentation.

Title: Parsed context may not reach the ranking model
Mitigation: List each context field and its availability, validation and use in ranking. Pass supported fields consistently and label unsupported conditions rather than implying they affect the result.
Linked work: Relates: SCRUM-539; Relates: SCRUM-540; Relates: SCRUM-526
Description:
Risk: Situational variables may be incomplete, noisy, or inappropriate for the target, weakening contextual recommendations.
Trigger: Features have poor coverage, unstable definitions, or no defensible contribution on held-out evaluation.
Assessment: the historical comment explicitly retained this concern.
Comments:
Actions:
* Reviewed available context features (score margin, time, recent events) when planning feature engineering.
* Kept context features limited for this iteration and treated ML uplift results cautiously.
Result:
* We are aware that context signal may be weak; this is reflected in how we explain limitations in the report.
Assessment:
* Probability remains medium.
* Impact medium; we will revisit if we extend feature engineering in later sprints.

Elaboration review: probability Moderate; impact Tolerable. Reviewed the assessment and updated the mitigation plan.
Next action: Create a feature inventory with definitions, availability, timing, and a held-out comparison for the proposed feature set.
Current mitigation result: not established by this planning update; record the actual observation after the check.
Next review: within seven days, or sooner if the trigger occurs.

The parser can recognize tactical conditions that never reach the ranking API. That makes the displayed situation look richer than the inputs actually used to rank plays.

Title: Poor calibration of predicted PPP
Mitigation: Track PPP bias and error by season and play type. Evaluate lagged predictors on untouched chronological holdouts before making forecasting claims; report small groups and unsupported results.
Description: Predicted PPP is systematically higher/lower than realized PPP.
Comments:
Actions:
* Ran quick checks comparing predicted PPP vs baseline PPP across sample plays.
* Looked at high-level distributions to verify predictions are in a reasonable range (no extreme unrealistic PPP values).
Result:
* No obvious calibration disasters detected, but we have not fully tuned calibration yet.
Assessment:
* Probability medium.
* Impact high; we explicitly call this out as a limitation when discussing ML vs baseline in the defence.

I added checks for whether predicted points per possession (PPP) are too high or too low, plus a comparison chart in SCRUM-476 ([b9f145d](https://github.com/Basketball-Capstone-25/NBAPlayRanker/commit/b9f145d15189dd7f6be6854166bce0aef3f58f01)). The calculation tests passed as part of the 176 backend tests, but I still need to check the analyst page in the browser. The model trains on earlier seasons and tests on later ones, but it still uses statistics from the season being tested, so this does not prove it can predict future games. The risk status is unchanged for now; [SCRUM-526](https://basketball-strategy.atlassian.net/browse/SCRUM-526) will test predictions using only information available beforehand.

I compared the calibration API results with the analyst page in SCRUM-476 and checked the calculations in BST-123/124. The report covers 1,650 test rows from five seasons, and its design is saved in Visual Paradigm revision 51.
I moved the risk back to Monitoring because the report still uses same-season statistics and does not prove how well this model or the other recommendation models will predict future games. I will keep checking whether predictions are too high or too low and whether each group has enough results; SCRUM-526 covers testing with information available before the prediction.

The calibration calculation passed its recorded checks, but it uses rates from the season being evaluated. The remaining work is to test predictions with information available before the prediction time.

The season-ahead model overpredicted by 0.02227 PPP on average, compared with 0.01845 for the prior-league baseline. Lower RMSE did not remove this bias. Keep Monitoring and check a separate later season before claiming good calibration. [Results](https://github.com/Basketball-Capstone-25/NBAPlayRanker/blob/ba814406a69c6de23f14af06a28f153eaa436fdc/docs/iteration-15/forecast/README.md).

Title: Models may overfit the available data
Mitigation: Compare training and untouched time-holdout error with strictly available predictors. Record model settings, sample size and baseline performance before changing model complexity.
Description: Model learns noise due to many features vs samples, hurting generalization.
Comments:
Actions:
* Used a season-wise time split for evaluation to reduce leakage from future to past.
* Compared training vs validation performance to look for large gaps.
Result:
* Early checks show some risk of overfitting but not catastrophic; we are not claiming production-grade generalization.
Assessment:
* Probability medium.
* Impact high; this remains an important limitation of the prototype model.

The earlier note acknowledged overfitting as a limitation, so Resolved is too strong. A season split alone does not establish generalization when the predictors include information from the evaluated season.

SCRUM-526 fixed eight features, chose Ridge alpha on an earlier tuning season and kept the final season outside selection. The 330 team/play-type rows are related observations from one season, so this does not establish generalization. Keep Monitoring until a separate later season is evaluated. [Split and limits](https://github.com/Basketball-Capstone-25/NBAPlayRanker/blob/ba814406a69c6de23f14af06a28f153eaa436fdc/docs/iteration-15/forecast/README.md).

Title: Data leakage inflates results
Mitigation: Define the prediction moment and whether each feature is observed, lagged or supplied as a planned action. Fit preprocessing on training data only and use an untouched time holdout. Do not present conditional or retrospective estimates as prospective accuracy.
Linked work: Relates: SCRUM-526; Relates: SCRUM-549; Relates: SCRUM-538
Description: Not using strict time splits leaks future info into training, inflating metrics.
Comments:
Actions:
* Reviewed feature engineering to avoid including direct outcome-like fields in the inputs.
* Used time-based splits to make sure future information does not leak into training.
Result:
* No obvious direct leakage features remain in the current feature set.
Assessment:
* Probability reduced to medium.
* Impact high if leakage is discovered later, so we continue to treat evaluation results as approximate.

I changed the calibration code so it calculates scaling and reliability values from the training seasons only ([b9f145d](https://github.com/Basketball-Capstone-25/NBAPlayRanker/commit/b9f145d15189dd7f6be6854166bce0aef3f58f01)). BST-123 passed the checks for keeping later-season results out of those calculations. The model still uses some statistics from the season being tested, which may not be available before a game. I am keeping this risk under Monitoring, with [SCRUM-526](https://basketball-strategy.atlassian.net/browse/SCRUM-526) covering tests that use only earlier information.

BST-123 passed the checks that keep training seasons separate from test seasons and prepare the data using training rows only. I checked that the analyst page explains these splits and limitations, with the design saved in Visual Paradigm revision 51.
The inputs still include statistics from the season being tested, so the earlier broad claims about preventing all data leakage are not proof of future-game accuracy. This risk stays under Monitoring, and SCRUM-526 remains To Do to check which inputs are available before a prediction.

Training and test seasons are separated, but the current diagnostic still uses same-season rate features. Keep the timing of every predictor in the next evaluation so future information cannot enter a forecasting claim.

The shot model uses the location and type of the shot actually taken, while BST-117 expects information available before the possession. Those inputs can describe conditional shot quality, but they do not establish a pre-possession forecast. Document the prediction moment and feature availability before the repaired dataset is used for holdout or cross-validation claims.

Changing the final season's points, possessions and rates left the selected model, fitted scaling and predictions unchanged in the new forecast tests. Inputs now come from the prior regular season. Monitoring remains because the CSV has no publication timestamps and the shot-model timing issue is separate. [Timing checks](https://github.com/Basketball-Capstone-25/NBAPlayRanker/blob/ba814406a69c6de23f14af06a28f153eaa436fdc/docs/iteration-15/forecast/README.md).

Title: ML model underperforms the baseline
Mitigation: Evaluate baseline and model on identical untouched examples. Report error and uncertainty, and retain the better-supported method when model gains are absent.
Description: XGBoost shows no uplift over the transparent scoring rule.
Comments:
Actions:
* Implemented deterministic PPP_pred and compared its RMSE to PPP_baseline on a hold-out set.
* Prepared visual/summary comparison to show the difference in performance during the defence.
Result:
* Current ML model is at least competitive with baseline on the tested split; we still emphasize limitations.
Assessment:
* Probability reduced but still medium.
* Impact medium; if ML underperforms we still have a strong baseline and can use the comparison as a learning point.

Uplift and calibration are implemented, but they do not settle whether the model improves future-game predictions over a baseline. Keep the baseline comparison open for the stricter evaluation.

Title: Shot events may be assigned to the wrong team
Mitigation: Recover authoritative raw events, map game participants explicitly and check team/opponent consistency. Rebuild derived shot data and verify samples against their raw events before trusting shot rankings.
Description: Timestamps/events don’t align cleanly with team/play-type rows; context features become noisy.
Comments:
Actions:
* Spot-checked several possessions across the raw Synergy export and the engineered dataset used by the model.
* Validated that play-type and PPP fields stay aligned for those samples.
Result:
* No major alignment errors found in the sampled rows.
Assessment:
* Probability now low.
* Impact high if present at scale, so we will re-check if we perform large data transformations later.

The shot-data audit found 18,746 rows with the same team and opponent and only one shooting-team label in every game group. The earlier sampled alignment result cannot support the current shot dataset.

Title: Small-sample play types distort rankings
Mitigation: Define a minimum possession threshold and test low-count groups. Show sample size or suppress unsupported rankings; do not treat extreme small-sample PPP as a strong recommendation.
Linked work: Relates: SCRUM-474; Relates: SCRUM-479; Relates: SCRUM-480
Description: Rare play types have few possessions and appear misleadingly strong/weak.
Comments:
Actions:
* Added a minimum sample size check when reviewing Top-K rankings (internally).
* Considered play types with extremely low counts as “noisy” and interpret them cautiously.
Result:
* Rankings used in the demo are not dominated by extreme small-sample outliers.
Assessment:
* Probability medium.
* Impact medium; documented as a limitation when we discuss interpretation of rankings.

Rare play types still need explicit sample checks even when the ranking calculation passes. Keep the minimum sample rule and warning visible instead of relying on an informal review of the demo teams.

Title: Player-to-team aggregation may calculate incorrect totals
Mitigation: Use known player rows to verify team possession totals and weighted PPP. Check duplicate player/team keys and compare the computed aggregate with the expected team result.
Description: Possession-weighted aggregation implemented incorrectly, skewing team stats.
Comments:
Actions:
* Confirmed that the main views in this iteration operate at team level, not individual player aggregation.
* For any roll-up examples, we manually verified that counts sum correctly for a small sample.
Result:
* No critical roll-up issues identified for the team-level views used in the demo.
Assessment:
* Probability now low for current scope.
* Impact medium if we add detailed player analytics later.

The Synergy pipeline already aggregates player rows into team and play-type results. Verify that current aggregation with a known possession-weighted fixture; displaying team-level outputs does not remove the risk of a bad roll-up.

Title: Invalid source data may produce misleading results
Mitigation: Validate game participants, team/opponent differences and expected shooting-team coverage as well as types and missing values. Block or visibly flag reports using failed data.
Linked work: Relates: SCRUM-538; Relates: SCRUM-479; Relates: SCRUM-480
Description: Non-numeric fields, NAs, or duplicates lead to wrong PPP or frequency values.
Comments:
Actions:
* Ran basic data quality checks (null counts, basic ranges) on the imported Synergy dataset.
* Ensured that obviously broken rows are excluded or handled safely by the preprocessing.
Result:
* Some missing values exist but do not break the pipeline; they are either dropped or defaulted safely.
Assessment:
* Probability medium.
* Impact medium; we treat data quality as a limitation and keep checks in place for future imports.

The current shot data contains invalid team/opponent pairs. Passing null and type checks did not catch that semantic error, so this risk is active again.

Title: Source changes may prevent dataset recovery
Mitigation: Keep raw extracts with source and schema versions. Validate required fields before replacing a working dataset, and retain the previous release for rollback.
Linked work: Relates: SCRUM-487; Relates: SCRUM-490; Relates: SCRUM-491; Relates: SCRUM-532
Description: hoopR/NBA tables or columns change (schema/rate limits), causing pulls or processing to fail.
Comments:
Actions:
* Captured the current dataset extract and froze it for the demo, instead of depending on live/uncontrolled updates.
* Documented the R/Notebook steps used to regenerate data if needed.
Result:
* Demo is stable against short-term data source changes.
Assessment:
* Probability now low for this release.
* Impact medium; if the upstream format changes, we would need to update preprocessing in a later sprint.

The frozen extract reduces dependency on live endpoints, but the original raw shot events were unavailable during diagnosis. That limits recovery if the source format or pull process changes.

Title: Limited expert feedback leaves coaching assumptions untested
Mitigation: Prepare three realistic coaching scenarios and specific questions. Record the reviewer, feedback and resulting changes, or clearly record that feedback is still pending.
Description: The project may miss practical coaching requirements when domain feedback is unavailable or not recorded.
Comments:
Actions:
* When designing the Top-K cards and tactics board, we based decisions on typical coach workflows (quick glance at best options, PPP_baseline).
* Adjusted terminology (e.g., “points per possession” and “play-type ranking”) to be understandable to basketball staff.
Result:
* Even without a full-time domain expert, we are aligning the UI with how coaches think.
Assessment:
* Probability remains medium (limited expert time).
* Impact medium; this is noted as a constraint in the project write-up.

The card has no description and no recorded expert review of the current app. Coach-friendly wording is useful, but it is not evidence that a domain expert validated the workflow.

Title: UI and API contracts may disagree
Mitigation: Keep the failed browser cases linked to their bugs. Verify parameters, access roles and response fields from the real page through the deployed API after each repair.
Linked work: Relates: SCRUM-544; Relates: SCRUM-545; Relates: SCRUM-539
Description: A page may send parameters, expect fields or allow roles that disagree with the backend contract.
Comments:
Actions:
* Tested the full flow from UI → baseline API → UI for Data Explorer and Top-K cards.
* Fixed mismatches in parameter names (season/team/opponent) where they were inconsistent.
Result:
* The main demo flows now run end-to-end without manual intervention.
Assessment:
* Probability reduced from high to medium.
* Impact high if new endpoints are added; for current scope, risk is acceptable.

The broader app audit found role mismatches, a response-shape crash and stale Gameplan inputs across the UI/API boundary. The earlier success on core pages does not cover these failing routes.

Title: Preprocessing may assign incorrect shot participants
Mitigation: Replace ambiguous column matching with explicit documented mappings. Preserve raw events, validate participants and row counts after each transform, and rebuild dependent artifacts only from verified input.
Description: Incorrect data mappings or cleaning rules may produce misleading features and recommendations.
Comments:
Actions:
* Reviewed preprocessing steps (filtering, feature engineering) to ensure they match the Synergy definitions.
* Kept the Data Explorer page close to raw data so we can visually verify the processed fields.
Result:
* Preprocessing for the baseline and current ML pipeline appears consistent and understandable.
Assessment:
* Probability now low.
